questions.stem: Which of the following best defines foreign direct investment?
options: Investment by a business in productive assets in another country
The purchase of shares in a foreign company for a financial return
The sale of goods to a customer in another country
A loan made by one government to another
questions.why: FDI means productive assets and normally a controlling interest, which distinguishes it from portfolio investment.
whyNot: That is portfolio investment.
That is exporting.
That is overseas aid or lending, not FDI.

questions.stem: Which of the following best defines specialisation?
options: Concentrating production on a narrow range of goods in which a country or business is relatively most efficient
Producing every good a country needs domestically
Selling the same product in many countries
Employing workers in more than one country
questions.why: Specialisation plus trade raises total output above what each producer could achieve alone.
whyNot: That is self-sufficiency, the opposite of specialisation.
That is international marketing.
That describes a multinational workforce.

questions.stem: Which of the following best defines a greenfield investment?
options: Building new facilities in a foreign country from scratch
Acquiring an existing business in a foreign country
Investing in environmentally friendly production
Exporting to a country for the first time
questions.why: Greenfield gives complete control over design, culture and standards, and starts with no customers or local knowledge.
whyNot: That is brownfield investment.
The term refers to new build, not to environmental credentials.
Exporting is not FDI at all.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a reason a business exports rather than only selling at home?
options: A saturated home market with only replacement demand
A rapidly growing home market with no competition
A desire to reduce total sales volume
An intention to avoid economies of scale
questions.why: Saturation, spare capacity, risk spreading and scale economies are the standard reasons.
whyNot: A growing uncontested home market is a reason to stay.
Businesses export to raise volume, not reduce it.
Higher volume brings scale economies, which is an attraction.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a cost of a country specialising heavily in one or two products?
options: Exposure to a price fall or a collapse in demand for that one thing
Lower total output than producing everything itself
The impossibility of trading with other countries
An automatic fall in living standards
questions.why: Specialisation raises efficiency and reduces resilience, and dependence is the price paid.
whyNot: Specialisation raises total output, which is why it happens.
Specialisation depends on trade rather than preventing it.
Living standards usually rise; the problem is vulnerability.

questions.stem: Why might a business choose FDI over exporting?
options: Tariffs and transport costs make exporting expensive, so producing inside the market avoids them
FDI requires less capital than exporting
FDI is easier to reverse than exporting
Exporting is illegal in most countries
questions.why: Producing inside the market also brings the business closer to the customer and may lower production costs.
whyNot: FDI requires far more capital.
FDI is largely irreversible, which is the central asymmetry in the decision.
Exporting is lawful and routine.

questions.stem: Which of the following is an advantage of brownfield over greenfield investment?
options: It is faster and brings existing customers, staff and local knowledge
It gives complete control over the culture of the new operation
It requires no integration effort
It avoids all political risk
questions.why: Brownfield buys speed and local relationships, at the cost of integration and culture-clash risk.
whyNot: Control over culture is the greenfield advantage.
Integration is the main brownfield risk.
Political risk applies to both.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a benefit of inward FDI for the host country?
options: Capital, jobs, technology transfer and tax revenue
A guaranteed permanent increase in wages across the economy
The elimination of all competition for local firms
A fall in the exchange rate
questions.why: It also puts pressure on local firms to raise their standards, though profits are repatriated and the investment may be footloose.
whyNot: Wage effects are real but not guaranteed or permanent.
Inward FDI usually increases competition for local firms.
Large inflows tend to raise the exchange rate, not lower it.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a criticism of inward FDI for a host country?
options: Profits are repatriated and the investment may leave when incentives end
It never creates any employment
It always reduces the country's GDP
It prevents the country from exporting
questions.why: The host government's bargaining position against a large multinational is also weak, which limits what it can extract.
whyNot: Employment creation is one of its clearest benefits.
FDI normally raises GDP.
FDI often increases exports from the host country.

questions.stem: Why are longer, more specialised supply chains described as efficient and fragile?
options: Each stage is highly efficient, and a disruption anywhere stops production everywhere
Longer chains always cost more to operate
Specialisation removes the need for suppliers
Fragility comes only from exchange rate movements
questions.why: This is the contingency planning point: efficiency and resilience trade off against each other.
whyNot: They are usually cheaper per unit, which is why they exist.
Specialisation increases the number of suppliers involved.
Currency risk is one of several fragilities, not the main one.

questions.stem: Why might a business locate an assembly plant inside a trade bloc rather than export into it?
options: A product assembled inside the bloc avoids the common external tariff
Production costs inside a bloc are always lower
Exporting into a bloc is prohibited
Trade blocs require all members to own local production
questions.why: The investment decision is driven by trade policy rather than by production cost, which is a useful example of protectionism changing business behaviour.
whyNot: Costs inside the bloc are often higher; the tariff is what tips the decision.
Exporting into a bloc is permitted, subject to the external tariff.
No such requirement exists in a bloc.

questions.stem: A business imports its inputs and sells at home. How is its exchange rate exposure different from an exporter's?
options: A stronger home currency helps it, whereas it would hurt an exporter
It has no exchange rate exposure at all
A stronger home currency hurts it, as it would an exporter
Its exposure depends only on interest rates
questions.why: SPICED: a strong currency makes imports cheaper, so the importer's costs fall while an exporter's products become dearer abroad.
whyNot: Imported inputs create real currency exposure.
The effects run in opposite directions for importers and exporters.
The exposure comes from the exchange rate, not interest rates directly.

questions.stem: What is the fundamental asymmetry between exporting and FDI?
options: Exporting is reversible while FDI is largely not
Exporting requires more capital than FDI
FDI avoids all regulation in the host country
Exporting cannot generate any profit
questions.why: That asymmetry is the heart of the decision, and it is why political stability matters far more for FDI than for exporting.
whyNot: FDI requires far more capital.
FDI brings the business fully within host-country regulation.
Exporting is a normal source of profit.

questions.stem: Which of the following best defines an import?
options: A good or service bought from a producer in another country
A good produced at home and sold abroad
A good produced and sold within the same country
A tax on goods entering a country
questions.why: Imports take money out of the country, while exports bring it in.
whyNot: That is an export.
That is domestic trade.
That is a tariff.

questions.stem: Why can specialisation raise a business's exposure to supplier power?
options: Concentrating on core activities means depending on fewer suppliers for the rest
Specialisation removes the need to buy anything
Specialised suppliers always charge less
Specialisation increases the number of alternative suppliers
questions.why: Dependence on a few suppliers raises their bargaining power, which is one of Porter's five forces.
whyNot: Specialisation increases reliance on bought-in inputs.
Specialists can charge more precisely because alternatives are scarce.
It usually reduces the number of viable alternatives.

questions.stem: Which product characteristic most favours producing locally rather than exporting?
options: Being bulky or perishable, so transport is expensive or slow
Being high in value and low in weight
Having a long shelf life
Being sold only online
questions.why: Transport cost and time dominate for bulky and perishable goods, while high-value low-weight goods are cheap to ship.
whyNot: Those goods are the easiest to export.
A long shelf life makes exporting easier.
Online sale does not by itself require local production.
